problems.description: 9 naming violations across 5 files (app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py): classes not PascalCase, functions not snake_case, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE. Naming is inconsistent especially in the newly added worker/repository modules, driving convention score to 0.67.

Greenfield rewrite collapses the seed's Blueprint-separated structure into a flatter single-module layout (app.py) alongside new modules, so module boundaries differ from the seed's existing patterns and from each other.
Type hints are used on some public signatures (get_db, init_db, get_task, task_dict) but not on all new public functions, so the convention is applied inconsistently.
Measurement reports 'Convention violations (9)' but only 8 violations are enumerated; the count and the list do not reconcile.

strengths: SonarQube delta is positive: -4 smells and -2 cognitive complexity with +0 bugs and +0.0% duplication — the rewrite is objectively cleaner than the seed.
Adopts timezone-aware datetimes (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) instead of the seed's deprecated datetime.utcnow().
Greenfield session includes test_app.py, so test coverage is carried forward rather than dropped.
Simpler surface area (+14 functions, -221/+155 lines) is a focused task-domain API rather than an over-generalized auth scaffold.
commit_reviews.summary: The commit improves static quality (fewer smells, lower complexity, no new bugs) but scores only 0.67 on conventions due to pervasive naming violations across the new modules, which introduces mild technical debt despite an overall better baseline than the seed.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me'; if deployed without the env var, tokens are forgeable with a publicly known secret.

Hand-rolled JWT (HMAC) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT: the header is never validated, exception handling has gaps, and payload is decoded before signature verification — correct here but brittle under future edits.
~80 lines of auth/token logic added inline to app.py rather than extracted into an auth module; the +16 functions and cognitive complexity +23 concentrate in a single file.
No tests added for register/login/token validity or the owner_id scoping, despite this being the security-critical surface of the change.
register/login and decode_token's inner paths lack return type hints; the project convention requires type hints on public signatures.
Bearer scheme check is case-sensitive; lowercase 'bearer' is rejected, which is safe but inconsistent with RFC 6750.

strengths: Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored plaintext.
Constant-time signature comparison via hmac.compare_digest with expiry validation.
Owner scoping applied to every task query, preventing cross-user data access.
Safe migration path using PRAGMA table_info before ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN.
Clean decorator-based auth via functools.wraps that slots into the existing route structure.
No new third-party dependencies added.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds idiomatic per-user ownership and token auth on top of existing patterns with real security care, but the hand-rolled JWT with a forgeable default secret and zero test coverage is the debt that tempers the score.

problems.description: Task dispatch is inline in the update_task route, coupling the request handler directly to Celery; a broker outage would surface as a 500 on a normal task-update call with no fallback.

celery_config.py routes the task to the 'notifications' queue, but nothing in the commit provisions a worker consuming that queue (default Celery queue is 'celery'), so enqueued messages could sit unconsumed in production.
send_notification_email.delay is invoked while the DB connection is still open inside the get_db() context manager, holding the connection during the enqueue round-trip.
Email is validated only for non-empty string, not format; malformed addresses are stored and enqueued.

Most of the 9 flagged violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants) are static-analysis false positives against framework conventions: Flask's lowercase 'app' instance and Celery's lowercase 'broker_url'/'result_backend' keys are idiomatic, so the 0.67 mechanical score understates true convention adherence.

strengths: Follows the existing schema-migration pattern (PRAGMA table_info + conditional ALTER TABLE) rather than forcing a fresh DB, preserving compatibility with legacy users.
Notification fires only on the status transition to 'completed' (status != 'completed' and status == 'completed'), correctly deduplicating repeated PATCHes and verified by a dedicated test.
Clean separation of Celery config into celery_config.py with env-driven broker URL and task routing, matching the project's env-driven configuration style.
New functionality is covered by a focused test using the existing monkeypatch/configure_database fixture conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent integration session that adds a Celery-backed notification path following existing migration, routing, and test patterns, with minor operational and coupling notes and a mechanical convention score that is skewed by framework-convention false positives.

problems.description: Repositories are re-instantiated per operation (TaskRepository(get_db) inside each route). Since the connection_factory is lazy, a module-level instance would be cleaner and avoids repeated object churn.

Generic BaseRepository.create/update interpolate column names from dict keys via f-strings, reducing type safety and surfacing typos only at runtime; values are typed as `object`. Column names originate from trusted internal call sites, so this is not a security issue.
BaseRepository ships unused generic CRUD (get_by_id, list_all, delete) that no caller exercises — mild YAGNI scaffolding for a small two-table app.

New repositories.py contributes a module-level constant naming violation; the 0.67 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py), so this commit is not the primary source of the low score.

strengths: Introduces the Repository pattern, isolating raw SQL and schema migration logic out of route handlers.
Behavior-preserving: SonarQube delta shows +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0 duplication, cognitive complexity +1 only.
Respects existing patterns by reusing the lazy get_db() connection factory and keeping task_dict/require_auth intact.
Centralizes schema creation and ALTER TABLE migrations in repository initialize() methods.
Reduces boilerplate in register, login, update_task, and list_tasks routes, improving readability.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving refactor that introduces the Repository pattern to isolate persistence from route handlers, at the cost of a slightly over-generic base class and minor convention noise.

problems.description: rate_limit_key() decodes and validates the JWT on every request (including non-auth routes that fall back to IP keying), adding crypto work to the hot path; a cached/auth-route-only key would be cheaper.

list_page_for_owner runs a COUNT(*) aggregate on every page request, and total + keyset pagination is a hybrid model; the total is unnecessary for cursor navigation and makes each page cost two queries.
Tests swap task_app.limiter._storage and _limiter by reaching into private attributes; a public storage swap helper or Limiter(app=...) fixture would be more robust.

Convention score 0.67 (9 violations) is dominated by pre-existing issues in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, module-level constant casing in repositories.py); this commit does not introduce those violations.

strengths: Rate limiting is properly scoped per-user (authenticated) and per-IP (anonymous), backed by Redis with a sane default, and wired through headers_enabled for client-visible limits.

Cursor (keyset) pagination avoids OFFSET performance degradation and is implemented via a new TaskRepository.list_page_for_owner that follows existing repository conventions (connection_factory, select_columns, typing).
Input validation for cursor and limit is explicit with clear 400 errors; next_cursor/total response shape is consistent across empty and non-empty results.
Strong test coverage added: pagination traversal, invalid pagination params, and rate-limit Retry-After behavior; SonarQube confirms zero new bugs/smells and zero duplication.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted cross-cutting session that adds production-grade rate limiting and cursor pagination following existing repository and route patterns, with the low convention score reflecting pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this commit.

compounding_issues: S2's hand-rolled JWT with a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me' fallback secret persisted through S5, where rate_limit_key() re-decodes the token on every request (hot-path crypto work and a forgeable token if deployed without JWT_SECRET)
S1's flat single-module layout left ~80 lines of auth logic inline in app.py; S4's repository refactor extracted only persistence, so auth stayed glued to routes and its debt was never decomposed

S3 inlined Celery dispatch in update_task with no worker provisioned for the 'notifications' queue, and coupled the app to Redis; S5 then reused that Redis dependency for rate limiting via a hardcoded default REDIS_URL

Naming/convention violations introduced in S1 (module-level constant casing, inconsistent naming) persisted into untouched files and kept the 0.67 convention score flat for S4 and S5 even though those commits were behavior-preserving

S4's generic BaseRepository builds SQL via f-string column interpolation from dict keys, reducing type safety (values typed as object) and leaving unused YAGNI CRUD that later sessions carried forward
key_decisions: S1: flat single-module rewrite that discarded the seed's Blueprint structure and token-table session auth in favor of a simpler task-domain API with timezone-aware datetimes
S2: hand-rolled HMAC JWT (no PyJWT) with per-user owner scoping enforced on every task query — the foundation that S4's get_for_owner/update_for_owner and S5's list_page_for_owner are built on
S2: safe schema evolution via PRAGMA table_info + conditional ALTER TABLE, a migration pattern S3 and S4 both reused
S3: Celery async email notification fired only on the status transition to 'completed', with env-driven broker config and task routing into a dedicated 'notifications' queue
S4: Repository pattern (TaskRepository/UserRepository) extracting all raw SQL and schema logic out of route handlers behind a lazy get_db() connection factory
S5: keyset cursor pagination avoiding OFFSET degradation plus per-user/per-IP Flask-Limiter rate limiting backed by Redis with explicit input validation
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the arc, with debt front-loaded into the first two sessions and then largely paid down. S1 was a net-positive rewrite (SonarQube: -4 smells, -2 cognitive complexity) but introduced naming violations and a flat layout; S2 added the security-critical auth surface with real care (werkzeug password hashing, constant-time comparison, owner scoping, safe migrations) yet shipped the most serious debt: a hand-rolled JWT with a forgeable default secret and zero auth tests. From there the arc sharpened: S3 was a clean Celery integration following existing patterns, S4 a behavior-preserving refactor (0 new bugs/smells, +1 complexity) that slimmed routes, and S5 the strongest commit — well-fitted cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination with dedicated tests. Review scores confirm the rise (architectural_fit 0.75/0.70/0.85/0.75/0.85; introduces_technical_debt true in S1–S2, false in S3–S5), test coverage grew steadily (5→10→11→11→15 passing), and code organized cleanly into app.py/repositories.py/notification_tasks.py — though the 0.67 convention score stayed pinned by S1-era violations in files later sessions never touched.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc — greenfield, auth, async integration, repository refactor, cross-cutting hardening — that improved steadily once S2's security debt (hand-rolled JWT, hardcoded secret) was contained, building cleanly to a polished S5 while leaving early-session convention and auth-structure debt only partially cleaned up.
